utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. The Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Josse and Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution, it's same composition as yesterday. All right. I understand that -- I need someone to write down the Polish surname which I find difficult to pronounce and I want to make sure that I pronounce it well. Mr. Bourgon, I understand you have some preliminary issue to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, judges, good afternoon, colleagues. Mr. President, we have looked carefully at what took place yesterday during the debates concerning the missing interview of 14, 15, 16, and 19 May 2003. And we believe, Mr. President, that further relief is required for the following reasons. This interview, pursuant to the Rules, 42 and 43, should have been recorded. What the Prosecution told us yesterday, it was a deliberate decision from them not to record this interview even though it was conducted in the room in which the equipment was available to conduct recorded interviews. We believe, Mr. President, that based on the information that we think came about in this interview, that simply saying that we do not have an audio is not sufficient. We are of the view that the Prosecution must have detailed notes of this interview which lasted four days, notes that go way beyond the three-page information report that we have received and we would ask, Mr. President, that the Prosecution be ordered to disclose their notes of an interview which was conducted deliberately contrary to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the first request we've had for any notes of any interview. I'll look into it and get back to us when I have a chance to look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, we promised you that first thing today we'll come down with our decision on your -- on the Defence joint motion, oral motion, for certification to appeal from our decision of yesterday, which, apart from confirming the existing protective measures, augmented same by decreeing that the proceedings or the testimony of this witness will take place in closed session. This is our oral decision. In our view, the impugned decision relates to two issues: The continuation or rescission of existing protective measures for Witness 116, and the augmentation thereof through the use of closed session. For clarity, I shall consider each of these points with reference to the two-pronged test for certification required and established by Rule 73. Our decision not to rescind the protective measures is based on the very particular facts before us relating to this specific witness. We therefore do not consider that the issue of the continuation of these measures, put in place by a previous Trial Chamber, is one that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. While it is unnecessary to go further, we are not of the opinion that the immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings either. With the protective measures of voice and face distortion, as well as pseudonym, the second issue relates to enhancing those protections by the use of closed session proceedings. Again, the Trial Chamber's decision on this point is premised entirely on the very particular circumstances of this witness, including the concerns which he outlined to the Trial Chamber yesterday when interviewed by us, combined with his testimonial history in this Tribunal. Therefore, once again we are of the opinion that the decision rendered does not raise an issue which meets either of the prongs, the two prongs, for certification. Finally, the Trial Chamber has further considered taking into account the arguments advanced by the Defence yesterday, whether the overall decision on protective measures for this witness is one which meets the test for certification. We have done so assuming that the witness is, as has been described by some of you, a very important Prosecution witness. However, we have come to the conclusion that even so, the decision to continue and augment his protective measures is not one that can be said to affect the fair and expeditious conduct of this trial. While public scrutiny is indeed an important protection, it is a matter that must be considered in terms of the trial overall and not with reference to a single witness. Accordingly, the joint Defence request for certification is hereby being denied. And I think we can now start. Mr. McCloskey, when do you think you will be able to come back with a reply for Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Probably by this evening or certainly tomorrow when I get a chance to look into it more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try not to delay it beyond early tomorrow, please. Thank you. I think you need to draw the curtains now. You didn't tell me yesterday that you agree with our interpretation of the protective measures, namely that there is no point in having the facial distortion and the voice distortion once we will be hearing the testimony in closed session. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with that, Mr. President. We do have I think the pseudonym sheet so we have that pseudonym number but otherwise, that seems fine. Also, and I have spoken to the Defence about it, we have some exhibits that we plan to show this witness and we have them in a binder in his language that we were going to provide to him so he can have easy reference to them so we are not locked into e-court. I don't think there has been any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. You need to tell me. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For my part I agree that there is no need for the additional measures. There were two or three things and I apologise for not raising them earlier. Firstly, I take it that in closed session there is really no restriction on how we refer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's perfectly okay to call him (redacted), et cetera. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I would tend to agree with you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We are in open session at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will redact that. There is no one outside but we will redact it for the purpose of delayed transmission in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The second point is an allied point. Although it will be appropriate to refer to him by name during his evidence, will we not need to assign a number to him for any further public documents? I assume he'll be PW-109, will he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's his number going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told 168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 168, okay. So that you will keep for your records.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the third point is, Mr. McCloskey referred yesterday to the witness's ability to speak English. I understand he speaks English rather well and if there is to be any debate as to the propriety of any line of questioning and the sort, he will need to leave the Chamber, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I mentioned that so that we knew that. I don't think he speaks it well but I think he understands it pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And this witness being who he is, and I think I won't be wrongly anticipating anything, I would suggest, Mr. McCloskey, while you are in direct, to avoid direct questions or leading questions because, otherwise, we'll start having objections and that would delay the proceedings. So try to avoid leading questions as much as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the first couple of questions I always start with. In this situation, this is a little different, is

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. It's when you come to the basics of his testimony. I saw you, Mr. Bourgon. Do you wish to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, concerning the documents that will be given to the witness while he testifies, I do agree with my colleague that this will make it much easier for him because he can feel the document and use it. However, not everybody in the courtroom has the paper copy and it makes a dig difference between what the witness is looking at and what we can look at. I've got the paper copies of most documents that the Prosecution has included on the list, but when we used to work with this old system at least everybody received a binder and when the Prosecution said that too, then everybody had the paper copy so we knew exactly what the witness had in his hands. That would be much preferable if my colleague wants to go back to the old system, that we be provided with copies and that goes for everybody in the courtroom so we know exactly what the witness is looking at. In the meantime if we can at least whenever he's going to refer to a document, to ensure that it is on the ELMO so we know exactly what he's looking at when he answers any specific questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Is there a reason why not all the Defence teams have a copy of this folder?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the time and effort it would have taken and this folder sometimes I vary from it, it's not something that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just convenience. I will not hurry through this so that we try to get this on the screen. And if I'm going too fast, please, let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could -- we need -- I can see we need another redaction from something I said, page 6, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid any redaction whatsoever, could we perhaps move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are just going to do that. Let's go into closed session straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
